scenes.text: Now. Where did I leave you, child? Tuesday evening, May thirty-first, 1921. A boy in a cell, a lie in the newspaper, a mob collecting like storm water. And Greenwood sitting down to supper, not knowing.

That headline ran at three o'clock. By dark it wasn't news anymore, it was scripture — every man repeating it added a verse. A rumor is a prayer to the wrong god, baby. And white Tulsa prayed it all night.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, dense crowd of men, hats, pushing forward
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, dense crowd of men, hats, pushing forward
scenes.text: By seven-thirty they were at the courthouse. By nine, near two thousand. Understand what a mob is, sugar: men who traded their minds for a mood. One fear, wearing a thousand hats.

Sheriff McCullough did his job that night. I will say it plain. Killed the elevator, barricaded the stairs, set riflemen up top, and told that crowd nobody was taking his prisoner. A rare man, holding a rare line.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, Greenwood men gathering outside a storefront office
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, Greenwood men gathering outside a storefront office
scenes.text: Word crossed the Frisco tracks, and Greenwood held council — at the Stradford, at the Tulsa Star where Mr. Smitherman ran his press. Veterans. France had taught them their lives were worth defending.

Twenty-five of them rode to the courthouse about nine, rifles honest on their shoulders, and offered the sheriff help protecting Dick. He turned them away polite, and they went home orderly. First trip. There were two.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, candlestick telephone, switchboard operator
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, candlestick telephone, switchboard operator
scenes.text: Then a telephone rang with a lie in it — the mob is storming the jail, somebody said. It wasn't so. Not yet. But fear don't check its sources, child. Fear just packs.

Seventy-five made the second trip, near ten o'clock. Against two thousand. Arithmetic did not matter anymore to men done kneeling. They offered once more. Once more, turned away. And on the turning away — it happened.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, courthouse crowd, jostling, faces close
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, courthouse crowd, jostling, faces close
scenes.text: An old white man grabbed at a tall veteran's pistol. What you doing with that gun, boy. Wrong man. Wrong night. Wrong word. They wrestled over it, and it went off.
One shot, child. To this day nobody can name whose finger. My daddy said later it didn't matter. Two thousand men had already fired it in their minds. That bullet was just catching up.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, night street chaos, muzzle flashes, men running
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, night street chaos, muzzle flashes, men running
scenes.text: The street came apart in seconds. Men died in the first minute of it, both colors. Ours fell back toward Greenwood fighting a rearguard the whole way, outnumbered twenty to one.

And white Tulsa went shopping. Broke into pawnshops and hardware stores and armed itself on credit it never meant to settle. They robbed their own stores to come kill us — and wrote us down as the criminals.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, police station steps, men milling
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, police station steps, men milling
scenes.text: The police station pinned badges on the mob. Special deputies, they called them. Told them to get a gun and get busy. The law didn't break that night, sugar. It enlisted.
By midnight the Frisco tracks were a battle line. Ours on the north side, theirs on the south. The same steel that had always told Tulsa who was who, now deciding who would live till morning.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, lamp-lit home interior, figures moving fast
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, lamp-lit home interior, figures moving fast
scenes.text: In our house, nobody slept. Men came carried and bleeding to Daddy's door, because the hospital was not for us. Mama's apron went dark by midnight. I was eight, rolling bandages, learning what a bullet asks of a body.

Daddy never raised his voice once, the whole night. Fear is a poor surgeon, Opal — that's all he said to me. Keep your hands slow. I have kept my hands slow through every terrible thing since. It works, child.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, automobile headlights racing dark residential street
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, automobile headlights racing dark residential street
scenes.text: Out in the dark, carloads ran our streets shooting into porches and windows. The first fires went up along Archer near one o'clock. When our firemen came, guns turned them back. Let it burn was the policy now.

From the upstairs window I watched a light lean on the sky and asked Mama was it morning already. No, baby, she said. That's not morning. First lie my mother ever told me. It surely was a kind of morning.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, silhouettes on rooftops and a grain elevator
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, silhouettes on rooftops and a grain elevator
scenes.text: Our men took positions where they could — the mill, the hill by the standpipe, the belfry of Mount Zion Baptist. That church was fifty-two days old, sugar. Dedicated in April, with a mortgage the size of heaven.
Remember that church. You and me are going to cry over her tomorrow. But that night her new brick held our watchmen and her basement held our prayers, and both of them were loaded.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, railyard before dawn, still and gray
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, railyard before dawn, still and gray
scenes.text: Toward four o'clock came a quiet like held breath. Thousands of armed men had ringed the tracks, waiting on a signal we did not know was coming. Machine guns set on the hills. Airplanes fueled at the field.
Some of our men prayed that hour. Some cleaned rifles. Don't let anybody tell you those are different activities, child. Not that night they weren't.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, locomotive releasing steam, whistle cord
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, locomotive releasing steam, whistle cord
scenes.text: Five oh-eight in the morning. June the first. A whistle screamed across the dark, long and mean, and two thousand throats answered it.
Whatever that whistle meant to the men who blew it, to us it meant one thing. The end of the world was punctual.

scenes.effective_query: 1920s archival film, men surging across tracks at a run, period recreation
scenes.original_query: 1920s archival film, men surging across tracks at a run, period recreation
scenes.text: They came across the tracks at a run, firing as they came. And behind them the sun rose red, child, like it was ashamed to be caught watching.
Daddy looked at Mama over my head and said, real quiet: Willa, put her shoes on. That's enough for tonight, baby. Next time — the morning the sky caught fire. You go on and rest now. I won't.

That was part two of Black Wall Street. Ten parts, one story, all here on this channel. If you came in late, go back and start with The Elevator. And meet me at part three, baby — the morning the sky catches fire.
